title: Aging‐Induced Ductile‐Brittle‐Ductile Transition in High‐Entropy Alloys and its Implications

recollection.starting_material: Guess: A solutionized single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy of the Cantor/CrCoNi family, likely CoCrFeMnNi or a closely related Al-containing variant such as Al0.3CoCrFeNi prepared to be largely FCC before aging.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Isothermal aging at intermediate temperatures (about 600–750°C) for varying durations (from under an hour to ~100–200 h), after homogenization/solutionizing and quenching, followed by mechanical testing (tensile, Charpy impact, possibly fracture toughness) and microstructural characterization (TEM, STEM-EDS, APT).
recollection.structure: Guess: Early-stage aging forms a near-continuous grain-boundary network of brittle intermetallics (either sigma phase in Cantor-type alloys or B2-NiAl-type in Al-containing HEAs) accompanied by fine intragranular ordered precipitates (L12/B2) a few nanometers in size. With prolonged aging, the GB films coarsen and break up into discrete particles (loss of percolation), while intragranular precipitates grow and become the dominant strengthening phase (sizes increasing from ~5–10 nm to ~40–80 nm), yielding an FCC matrix with a dispersed ordered-precipitate population and discontinuous GB particles.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: The ductile–brittle–ductile sequence arises from competing effects of precipitation. Initially (solutionized), the FCC matrix has high work-hardening and ductility. Short/early aging generates continuous or semi-continuous brittle GB films that drastically reduce GB cohesion, promote intergranular fracture, and trigger a brittle response despite higher strength. With further aging, GB phases coarsen and lose continuity (reducing intergranular crack percolation), while intragranular ordered precipitates (L12/B2) increase in size/volume fraction, enhancing work hardening and potentially lowering SFE to activate TWIP/TRIP-like mechanisms, thereby restoring ductility while maintaining elevated strength.
recollection.results: Guess: Mechanical properties show a time-dependent minimum in ductility/impact resistance. As-solutionized: YS ~300–400 MPa, UTS ~700–800 MPa, total elongation ~50–70%, Charpy ~100–200 J. Short aging (e.g., 650°C for 1–4 h): YS ~900–1100 MPa, UTS ~1000–1200 MPa, elongation drops to ~2–5%, Charpy <10 J, intergranular fracture; fracture toughness K (or J) falls markedly (e.g., to ~20–30 MPa√m equivalent). Long aging (e.g., 650°C for 50–100 h): YS ~800–900 MPa, UTS ~900–1100 MPa, elongation recovers to ~20–35%, Charpy ~40–80 J, with mixed or ductile fracture and toughness partially restored (e.g., ~50–80 MPa√m equivalent). Microstructurally, precipitate size increases from ~5–10 nm to ~40–80 nm and GB film continuity decreases strongly, correlating with the ductility recovery. The paper likely emphasizes design implications: avoid continuous GB films, favor intragranular ordered precipitates, and define aging windows that balance strength, ductility, and toughness.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies intermediate-temperature aging in roughly the 600–750°C range. However, it misidentifies the initial microstructure and replaces the actual L12 ordering/jagged FCC–B2 phase-boundary evolution with a speculative grain-boundary-film and precipitate-coarsening scenario. Consequently, its proposed intergranular-fracture/percolation mechanism is inconsistent with the reported APBE/modulus-driven planar slip, phase-boundary stress concentration, and ductile transition zones. The numerous mechanical-property and precipitate-size values are unsupported guesses.
